title: Foreign supplier delays have become more closely linked to producer inflation while evidence on GDP spillovers is less decisive
bank: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
summary: Delays at a country’s foreign suppliers have become more closely associated with its own inflation since 2023. The relationship is especially strong for producer prices. Evidence that trade in intermediate inputs now also ties countries’ economic cycles more closely together is less conclusive. These are separate findings from a Federal Reserve staff note by Francois de Soyres. The author measures how prices and activity move across economies. He makes no monetary policy recommendation and does not estimate how an individual country would respond to a particular disruption.

For inflation, the study uses quarterly data for 15 economies through the second quarter of 2026. Manufacturers report whether their suppliers’ delivery times have lengthened or shortened, and the index is signed so that a higher reading means more stress. A domestic measure uses the country’s own responses; a foreign measure weights trading partners by their shares in the country’s intermediate-input imports. A global index substitutes for partners without manufacturing survey data. The regressions account for domestic slack, lagged inflation, oil prices and persistent differences across countries. Delivery times can lengthen because of strong demand as well as an interruption in supply. The appendix also clarifies that the series labelled CPI is an OECD private-consumption price index, a deflator proxy rather than each country’s headline CPI.

Figure 1 gives an economic scale for the domestic relationship. In the full sample, a one-standard-deviation rise in own delivery times, about 6.7 index points, is associated with annual consumer price inflation 0.19 percentage point higher and producer inflation 0.82 point higher. For a one-standard-deviation rise in the output gap, about 2.7 percentage points, the corresponding estimates are 0.11 and 0.13 point. These are like-for-like comparisons of historically sized changes, not of equal numerical changes in the two indicators.

Figure 2 gives coefficients per one-point increase in foreign delivery-time stress. For consumer prices the estimate rises from 0.006 percentage point before 2020 to 0.080 since 2023; for producer prices it rises from 0.035 to 0.449. The changes are significant at the 1% level. The two subperiods exclude 2020–22, and the later one contains 204 country-quarters. Domestic and foreign measures enter separate regressions: their correlation rose from 0.35 to 0.83, so the estimated effects cannot be added. Ending the recent sample in 2025 leaves a strong producer-price estimate of 0.856, but consumer prices give 0.084 with a p-value of 0.32. The short-sample qualification matters most when drawing conclusions about prices paid by households.

The output exercise compares 325 pairs of economies over rolling ten-year windows. Figure 3 relates the correlation of their GDP cycles to the logarithm of bilateral intermediate-input trade relative to combined GDP, controlling for portfolio links and country-pair characteristics. The estimated coefficient is 0.114 before 2020 and 1.029 in the two latest windows ending in 2023 and 2024. That is a slope on log trade intensity, not a correlation above one. The latest estimate has a wide 90% interval of roughly 0.15–1.91. The author smooths the 2020–21 GDP shock before filtering; removing 2020–22 altogether lowers the slope to 0.890 with a p-value of 0.25. Dropping the portfolio control leaves a similar pattern. The apparent strengthening is sensitive to how the pandemic enters the calculation.

Sourcing geography helps explain why exposure might persist even when bilateral routes change. Figure 4 uses all goods imports, a different dataset from the intermediate-input weights, which are frozen at 2022 values thereafter. Of 13 economies with observations for 2025, nine experienced changes smaller than 0.005 in their source-concentration index since 2019, yet China’s import share rose in ten. The US share sourced from China fell from 18.4% to 9.3%, and Mexico became the largest direct supplier. Customs origin may conceal upstream ownership or inputs. The appendix’s country results also caution against applying a common pass-through coefficient to an individual company or economy. A new shipping route need not remove the underlying exposure, and exposure to a common supplier does not identify who ultimately absorbs higher costs.

questions.question: Does supplier stress improve real-time forecasts of consumer inflation as well as producer inflation?
questions.detail: Rebuild the partner-weighted index with only the survey releases and import weights available at each forecast date. Compare forecast errors with a domestic-slack model and with the global pressure index, across both consumer and producer prices. The recent consumer estimate is sensitive to its endpoint. Confirmation out of sample would matter for inflation-linked holdings more directly than confirmation for producer prices alone.

questions.question: Where does a change of import origin leave exposure to the same upstream producer?
questions.detail: Compare customs origin with OECD input-output linkages, supplier ownership and firms’ disclosed sourcing for products shifted from China to Mexico or Vietnam. Separate new production capacity from routing changes or production by the same parent. That distinction would determine whether a portfolio diversified by direct supplier country is still exposed to a common shortage.

questions.question: Are countries with strong production links genuinely losing diversification benefits?
questions.detail: Repeat the GDP comparison with additional non-pandemic observations and non-overlapping windows. Test whether conclusions survive removing the largest common suppliers and controlling for common demand. The paper measures GDP comovement, not asset returns. For a cross-country portfolio, then check whether related earnings revisions or credit losses move together once common market repricing is accounted for.
